To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of dynamic parameterized abstractions in hierarchical proof planning can improve the e ciency of proof search and thus the e ectiveness of proof planning in the context of industrial applications.
we have designed and implemented a dynamic parameterized abstraction that is used in the proof search of a proof planner and that we have evaluated this approach with a number of case studies.
we have developed a new technique for proof planning, which allows to cope with the size of industrial case studies by using dynamic abstractions of the proof space.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following issues: 1.

the following questions How can we use abstractions to support hierarchical proof search How can we guide this search by heuristics How can the search space be controlled to avoid combinatorial explosion

the following questions 1 How to decompose a given goal into several sub-goals in order to obtain an abstract proof 2 How to choose an appropriate abstraction for each of these sub-goals 3 How to guide the search for an abstract proof 4 How to reconstruct the proof of the original goal from the abstract proof
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proof-planning approach presented in this paper is a promising tool for the application of formal verification techniques in an industrial setting
the use of parameterized abstractions is a promising way to cope with the problem of large case studies in the context of proof-planning
the use of dynamic parameterized abstractions is an interesting new technique which is applicable to proof-planning systems and which has the potential of improving the proof search.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have been able to prove a number of large case studies in the field of safety-critical systems and that we have been successful in proving theorems in the presence of large terms and complex formulae.
the combination of hierarchical proof planning with dynamic abstraction techniques allows us to handle large case studies and to apply formal methods to industrial size problems
our approach allows the application of a proof planner to a larger set of problems than it could handle before without any loss of e ciency
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of dynamic abstractions and the decomposition of goals into subgoals can lead to a substantial reduction of the proof search space and therefore to a substantial reduction in the proof search time
dynamic parameterizations of abstract terms allow to guide a proof search in a more flexible way compared to the use of static parameterizations

we have been able to apply our techniques to a large case study in the domain of safety-critical systems and have shown that the hierarchical proof planning approach together with the use of dynamic abstractions is very promising to tackle large case studies.
